Stage 1 is done. I pulled 3,640 records from OpenAlex and kept 2,810 research papers. Each kept paper has its authors, their institutions and country codes, `counts_by_year`, and the five-year citation count. Nothing is committed yet.

**Pulled / kept, by journal and year**

| | 2008 | 2009 | 2010 | 2011 | 2012 | 2013 | 2014 | 2015 | 2016 | 2017 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ASQ | 62/20 | 76/18 | 65/15 | 51/17 | 47/16 | 57/17 | 51/28 | 40/19 | 51/23 | 54/35 | 554/208 |
| AMJ | 68/55 | 69/54 | 92/64 | 73/53 | 136/124 | 75/68 | 85/77 | 92/86 | 93/89 | 92/87 | 875/757 |
| SMJ | 97/82 | 102/86 | 87/72 | 88/73 | 101/86 | 202/187 | 147/125 | 145/128 | 152/100 | 147/103 | 1268/1042 |
| OrgSci | 97/85 | 88/71 | 112/98 | 119/111 | 82/77 | 102/84 | 72/67 | 110/77 | 88/70 | 73/63 | 943/803 |

**Decisions you should check:**

1. **Wrong ISSN for Organization Science.** 0170-8406, the ISSN in `notes.md`, is *Organization Studies*. I pulled Organization Science with its correct ISSN, 1047-7039. If you actually meant Organization Studies, tell me and I'll re-pull.
2. **Year means first appearance online.** OpenAlex's publication year is when a paper first appeared online, not its print issue year. As a result, a journal-year can mix two or three print volumes. AMJ 2012 and SMJ 2013 look inflated because both journals started posting papers online before print around then. It also shifts which papers fall inside 2008–2017 at the edges. Using that year as the start of the citation window is defensible. If you'd rather define the sample by print volume, that's a small change.
3. **Citations before 2012 come from a second query.** OpenAlex's `counts_by_year` only goes back to 2012, so for papers from 2008–2011 it can't build the window on its own. For the missing years I counted citing papers by their publication year, using a separate OpenAlex query. That query matched `counts_by_year` closely on the years I compared. Per your definition, the window covers the publication year plus the five following years, so it is six calendar years.
4. **The type filter wasn't enough.** Many non-research items in OpenAlex are labelled "article", so I added rules. Every dropped record is listed with its reason in `data/excluded.csv`.
   - **Japanese journal mixed in:** OpenAlex has merged the Japanese journal 組織科学 (*Soshiki Kagaku*) into Organization Science. Its papers are dropped because their DOIs belong to that journal or are missing.
   - **ASQ and AMJ short items:** anything of 11 pages or fewer, or with no page numbers, is dropped. In these two journals those were all book reviews, editors' essays or special-issue introductions.
   - **SMJ and Organization Science short items:** only items of 3 pages or fewer are dropped. This removes errata and editors' notes, but also a few short commentaries and replies. Longer commentaries and replies are still in the data.
   - **Duplicates:** where the same title appears twice in a journal, I kept one record. The other was an erratum or a second DOI for the same paper.
   - **SSRN DOIs:** 11 real AMJ, ASQ and SMJ papers exist in OpenAlex only under an SSRN DOI, so I kept them.
   - **Your listed exclusions:** OpenAlex's own non-research flag and types caught front matter, book reviews, editorials, errata and retraction notices. I also dropped 5 records for retracted papers and 4 meta-analyses that OpenAlex labels "review" rather than "article". Say if you want the meta-analyses back.

**For later stages:**
- **Two-letter country codes:** OpenAlex uses US/GB, not the three-letter USA/GBR that `notes.md` assumes. The World Bank join will need a conversion step.
- **Missing countries:** 82 papers have at least one author with no institution country.
- **Draft methods paragraph:** it says a 3-year window, not 5.
- **Wuchty et al.:** the paper is 2007, not 2005.
- **OpenAlex's origin:** OpenAlex replaced Microsoft Academic Graph, not Google Scholar.

I built `data/clean/papers_clean.csv` with 2,810 rows, one per paper, using `code/clean.py`. The log is in `output/cleaning_log.txt`. I haven't run any models yet.

| Step | Papers |
|---|---|
| Read from `papers.jsonl` | 2,810 |
| Exact-duplicate DOIs dropped | 0 |
| Team-size sample (all papers) | 2,810 |
| International variable missing (no author has a country) | 6 |
| Country sample | 2,804 (1,220 international, 1,584 single-country) |

No exact DOI duplicates were left. Stage 1 had already removed the one near-duplicate pair (`amj.2011.0345` / `amj.2011-0345`) by title; an exact-DOI check would not have caught it.

**Variables:** `cites_5yr`, `n_authors` (raw), `n_authors_top8` (for the models), `journal`, `year`, `n_countries`, `international`. I also kept these for checking: `openalex_id`, `doi`, `n_authors_no_country`, `countries`.

- **Author counts:** most papers have 1–4 authors. The top-code only affects 2 papers, with 12 and 17 authors.
- **Authors without a country:** 91 of 7,102 authorships, spread across 84 papers. They stay in the author count but don't add a country.
- **Where countries come from:** only the authors' listed institutions, as you specified. OpenAlex also has its own per-author country field; it disagrees with the institutions for just 2 authors.

Two consequences of counting an author in every country they're affiliated with:
- **117 of the 1,220 international papers** are international only because some author has institutions in two countries. Counting each author's first-listed institution only, they would be single-country.
- **19 solo-authored papers** are coded international.

That follows your rule, but it partly mixes up having more coauthors with simply having more affiliations, which matters for H2. For a robustness check, the simplest option is to count only each author's first-listed institution. I can add that as an alternative variable if you want it.

The journal-by-year imbalances from stage 1 carry through unchanged: the jumps in AMJ 2012 and SMJ 2013, and the thin ASQ counts of 15–35 papers a year.

Stage 3 is done. `any_nonhigh` is now in `data/clean/papers_clean.csv`, and the country table is at `output/tables/countries_income.csv`. The FY2017 income groups are rebuilt from World Bank data rather than taken from its official classification file, which I couldn't download.

**How the FY2017 groups were built**
- **Blocked hosts:** the official historical file, `OGHIST.xlsx`, was blocked on both `databankfiles.worldbank.org` and `datacatalogfiles.worldbank.org`. The World Bank blog and data help desk were blocked too.
- **The rebuild:** through the World Bank API (`api.worldbank.org`), I pulled 2015 GNI per capita (Atlas method) from the July 2016 data release, which is the release the FY2017 groups were set from. Each country's group is set against the FY2017 thresholds:

  | Group | 2015 GNI per capita (US$) |
  |---|---|
  | Low | 1,025 or less |
  | Lower-middle | 1,026–4,035 |
  | Upper-middle | 4,036–12,475 |
  | High | 12,476 or more |

- **Unverified thresholds:** I couldn't check those thresholds against a World Bank page, because the hosts that publish them are blocked; they are from my own knowledge. As a check, the results match the FY2017 groups I know for Russia (upper-middle, 11,400), Hungary (high, 12,990) and Argentina (upper-middle, 12,460). Lebanon comes out upper-middle, which is correct for FY2017 even though it is lower-middle today.
- **Code mapping:** the two-letter to three-letter conversion comes from the World Bank API's country list. Taiwan was added by hand as TWN.

**Countries classified by hand** (each has a reason in the table's `note` column)
- **Taiwan:** not in the World Bank data, so classed high income, as you asked.
- **Argentina:** upper-middle. Its 2015 value first appears in the October 2016 release, at 12,460, which is under the high-income cut-off.
- **Macao:** high. Its 2014 value is 76,300 and its 2015 value is 67,180.
- **Iran:** upper-middle. No 2015 value exists; its 2014 value is 6,550.
- **Cuba:** upper-middle. There's no GNI value for any year, so this is the World Bank's current group, not an FY2017 figure.

**Results**
- **Countries:** the 54 sample countries split into 35 high, 14 upper-middle and 5 lower-middle income. None are low income.
- **The new variable:**

  | `any_nonhigh` | Papers |
  |---|---|
  | 1 | 160 |
  | 0 | 2,644 |
  | Missing | 6 (the same 6 papers already missing `international`) |

- **Mostly China:** most of the 160 come from China (90 papers) and India (27).
- **Small cells:** 151 of the 160 are also international papers. Only 9 papers are single-country papers from a non-high-income country. Keep that in mind when interpreting this variable alongside the international variable in the models.

Two things to know before re-running:
- **Run order:** run `code/clean.py` first, then `code/income.py`. `clean.py` rewrites the clean file without `any_nonhigh`.
- **Sources saved:** the raw World Bank downloads are in `data/external/`, along with `iso2_to_iso3.csv` and `wb_income_fy2017.csv`.

If you can get `OGHIST.xlsx`, it's worth checking these groups against it. The likeliest disagreements are Argentina, Cuba and Iran.

Stage 4 is done and all six models converged. Larger teams get more five-year citations, and international teams get more again beyond team size. Having a non-high-income author shows no effect. The script is `code/analysis.py`; tables are in `output/tables/` and figures in `output/figures/`.

**Main models** (incidence rate ratios; robust HC1 standard errors in parentheses)

| | Model 1 | Model 2 | Model 3 | Model 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Authors (top-coded at 8) | 1.083*** (0.018) | | 1.064*** (0.018) | 1.065*** (0.018) |
| International | | 1.158*** (0.041) | 1.114** (0.041) | 1.119** (0.042) |
| Any non-high-income author | | | | 0.962 (0.057) |
| N | 2,810 | 2,804 | 2,804 | 2,804 |
| Log-likelihood | −14,234.4 | −14,207.6 | −14,198.8 | −14,198.6 |

- **H1 (team size):** each extra author goes with about 8% more five-year citations, or about 6% once international is controlled.
- **H2 (international):** international papers get about 11% more citations than single-country papers of the same team size, significant at p < 0.01.
- **Extension (non-high-income author):** no effect. The ratio is 0.96 and not significant, and adding the variable barely changes the log-likelihood. Only 160 papers have such an author, and just 9 of those are single-country papers.

**Robustness check (each author's first-listed institution only):** the international effect gets smaller but is still significant at p < 0.05. The ratio is 1.086 in Model 3 and 1.092 in Model 4. The non-high-income ratio is 0.94 and still not significant. The sample stays at 2,804 papers because no paper loses all its countries under this rule. The change comes from 117 papers that drop from international to single-country, and 16 that drop from 1 to 0 on the non-high-income variable.

**Descriptives:** mean five-year citations are 65.8 (SD 62.7, median 47, maximum 628). Papers have 2.5 authors on average; 43.5% are international and 5.7% have a non-high-income author. The largest correlation is 0.29, between author count and international. With citations, the correlations are small: 0.09 for author count and 0.06 for international.

**What the figures show**
- **Figure 1:** citations rise from about 53 for solo papers to about 65 for teams of 2–3 and about 82 for teams of 4. The bars for 7 and 8+ authors rest on only 4 papers each, so their intervals are very wide. The 7-author interval runs below zero and is clipped at 0.
- **Figure 2:** the international advantage only shows up at 3 or more authors. With 2 authors it is slightly reversed (66 vs 64). With 4 or more it is large (87 vs 69). Model 3 assumes one international effect for every team size, so a team-size × international interaction would be a natural addition. I haven't run it.

**How the models were set up**
- **Model type:** NB2 negative binomial with dispersion estimated by maximum likelihood. Standard errors on the ratios are by the delta method.
- **Author count is linear:** each extra author is assumed to add the same percentage. Figure 1 shows the actual pattern isn't a straight line.
- **Year fixed effects:** these use OpenAlex's year, which is the year the paper first appeared online.
- **LaTeX table:** pandas' LaTeX export needs `jinja2`, which isn't installed, so the script writes the LaTeX itself.
